lesson.text: Quick memory: what does SET do to a variable? (It puts a value in it, replacing what was there before.) Today: the types of data a variable can hold.
A variable is a named box for a value. Its data type says what kind of value it holds, so the computer knows what it can do with it.
An integer is a whole number, like 3, 0 or −12. Integers are good for counting: lives, gems, a level.
A real number (a decimal) has a decimal point, like 2.5 or 9.81. Reals are good for measuring: speed, height, time.
A string is text inside quotes, like "Pip" or "Game over": good for names and messages. A Boolean is just TRUE or FALSE: good for yes-or-no things like has_key.
The type matters. 5 + 5 adds two numbers and makes 10, but "5" + "5" joins two strings side by side and makes "55".
Worked example: SET gems TO 7, then CHANGE gems BY 3, and gems holds 10. Then SET gems TO 2 replaces it: gems holds 2, not 12.
Try it in the world: list the variables a game like this one needs, from your gold to whether it is night, and give each its type. Next: complex decisions.

exercises.hint: Does it have a decimal point or quotes?
exercises.explain: 42 is a whole number with no decimal point or quotes: an integer.
Letters in quotes are a string: text.

exercises.prompt: What type of data is TRUE?
exercises.hint: Which type has only two values?
exercises.explain: TRUE is a Boolean: it can only be TRUE or FALSE.
True: it has a decimal point.

exercises.prompt: What is lives when the program ends?
Sort these values into their types.
exercises.hint: Quotes make text, even round digits. TRUE and FALSE alone are true or false.
exercises.explain: Numbers: 42 and 2.5. Text: "hello" and "7" (in quotes). True or false: TRUE and FALSE.

exercises.hint: Are they numbers or strings? + joins strings.
exercises.explain: They are strings, so + joins them side by side: 123.

exercises.prompt: Match each variable to the best type for it.
exercises.explain: lives counts (integer), a name is text (string), speed is measured (real) and has_key is yes or no (Boolean).

exercises.prompt: What is score when the program ends?
exercises.hint: Work out score + bonus with the values in the boxes.
exercises.explain: score + bonus is 10 + 5 = 15, and SET puts 15 in score.

exercises.prompt: "7" in quotes is a number that the computer can add up.
exercises.explain: False: in quotes it is a string of text. Take the quotes away to make it a number.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best type for a player's height in metres?
exercises.hint: Heights are measured and can have parts of a metre.
exercises.explain: A height like 1.45 m has a decimal point: a real number.

exercises.hint: Are a and b numbers or strings? Look for quotes.
exercises.explain: a and b hold the strings "3" and "4", so + joins them: 34.

exercises.prompt: What is y when the program ends?
exercises.hint: SET y TO x copies the value x has at that moment.
exercises.explain: y gets a copy of 5. Changing x to 9 later does not change y: y is 5.

exercises.prompt: A Boolean can hold three values: TRUE, FALSE and MAYBE.
exercises.hint: How many values has a switch?
exercises.explain: False: a Boolean is only ever TRUE or FALSE.

exercises.hint: Test each side of OR with the values, then join them.
exercises.explain: has_key = TRUE is false, but gems > 3 is true (4), and OR needs one: Gate opens.

exercises.prompt: What is count when the program ends?
exercises.hint: Trace it: the loop first, then the last line.
exercises.explain: The loop adds 2, 3 times: 3 × 2 = 6. Then count * 10 is 60.

exercises.prompt: Why does a program need data types?
choices: so it knows what it can do with each value
exercises.explain: The type tells the computer whether to add, join or test a value.
